nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: The engine looks for the pattern on the left, and replaces it with the one on the right.
nodes.statement: PuzzleScript's directly retrieved Rules 101 documentation describes a working engine in which creators express tile-based puzzle behavior through pattern-replacement rules. Examples change pushing, movement, disappearance and teleportation. It also shows a rule that causes an infinite loop and explains a manual correction. This establishes executable rule-based authoring, not automatic verification across all states, creator-facing counterexamples, or routine commercial publishing by nonprogrammers. The page is undated; its cutoff version was not independently checked.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: No public shows are available at this time.
nodes.statement: Adventure Lab's directly retrieved site offers VR adventures with live improvisational performers, paying guests, up to eight players and a 60-minute format. It says performers guide the adventure and react to the team. However, the same page says no public shows are currently available and directs private-show inquiries to email. It establishes an actual paid human-hosted game arrangement, not verified current bookings, recurring profitability, multiple sustainable businesses, or live alteration of geometry and objectives. The page is undated and its current booking operation was not independently checked.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: If a player must leave early, they can use Archipelago's release system.
nodes.statement: Archipelago's directly retrieved FAQ explains cross-game multiplayer in which finding an item in one game sends it to another player's different game, affecting progress. Users can generate and host experiences; developer documentation and example game implementations are linked. A release system sends a departing player's outstanding items so others can continue. Generation rules aim to keep necessary items accessible. This is a strong existing analogue for consequential cross-game composition, including a departure fallback. It does not establish host-operator permission for every integration, general world-state editing, comprehensive version guarantees, or recovery from every host outage. The documentation is undated.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.statement: An inspected source-extracted search result from Second Life's llRequestPermissions documentation describes executable scripts requesting permission for consequential actions, including taking money, controlling avatars, changing links, teleporting and returning objects. Permissions persist across script state changes but have specific limits, including one agent per script. This supports existing permission-controlled behavior inside a shared world, not evidence that ordinary players supply most new activities, that creations have durable shared dependencies, or that abandoned systems can be transferred and repaired. Direct retrieval of the related creation documentation failed. Page date and exact cutoff version remain unverified.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: These activities continue even after world generation, as you play the game.
nodes.statement: The directly retrieved Dwarf Fortress Wiki world-generation page describes simulated geography, civilizations and character histories that shape starting conditions and continue during play. Creators or players can select history length and interrupt generation when desired conditions occur; longer histories change the surviving settlements, creatures and other available features. This is an existing mechanism for obtaining playable situations from simulated history. The retrieved portion does not establish large-batch searches in multiple commercial production pipelines, comprehensive causal debugging, or specific unanticipated player solutions. The community page identifies a current game version but warns some content may need updating; its cutoff version was not checked.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: The behavior code is compiled without developer intervention and the resulting object is incorporated into the game.
nodes.statement: The 2024 GROMIT paper reports a Unity system that generates behavior code when a player initiates an interaction, compiles it without developer intervention and incorporates the result into play. Its evaluation reports downstream gameplay effects; interviews with 13 developers identify concerns about quality, community expectations and workflow, and the paper calls for additional guardrails. This is a stronger existing analogue than fixed-schema object generation: runtime executable behavior invention itself is already demonstrated in research. The inspected excerpt does not establish multiple paid games, generated locations, multi-session persistence or primarily constraint-based production. Direct PDF fetch failed because the response exceeded the buffer; these claims come from substantive source-extracted search text, with full evaluation context unverified.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: A playable build of the developed software artifact is provided for Windows x64.
nodes.statement: The Real-Time World Crafting project README describes a 2D spell-crafting prototype in which a language model translates player commands into a restricted instruction language that configures object behavior at runtime. It reports model and prompting comparisons and offers a Windows build requiring the player's own API key. This supports an existing constrained runtime-programming mechanism, not verified security, sustained paid use, multi-session persistence or a commercial authoring workload. Direct repository fetch failed to complete; the substantive README was inspected through source-extracted search text. The README's publication date and exact cutoff version were not verified.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: a single, concise game definition to get both a playable prototype and a formal rule system
nodes.statement: The 2009 BIPED demonstration reports that one concise game definition produces both a playable prototype and a formal rule system. Designers can request complete play traces satisfying additional constraints, exposing exploits and puzzle solutions. This is a stronger existing analogue than manual rule execution alone. It does not establish complete commercial releases, all-state verification or mandatory conflict resolution by nonprogrammers. The substantive abstract was retrieved through source-extracted search text; direct fetch failed with a storage/Unicode error. The full implementation and evaluation were not inspected.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: to both produce a winning sequence of actions and to formally verify custom game design properties
nodes.statement: Onur Tekik's November 2021 thesis describes generating and verifying maze-like game levels using the SPIN model checker. Its abstract reports custom game-design property checks, automated tailoring of template models to levels, counterexample-generated solutions and animation through PyVGDL. This establishes prior research on formal game-property checks and visible traces, not an end-to-end commercial nonprogrammer builder or proof that all proposed projects can be exhaustively checked. Direct PDF fetch failed; the inspected source-extracted search text contained the title, date, abstract and contents, but not the full results.

nodes.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
nodes.quote: Tool for extracting source code from exported standalone games
nodes.statement: PuzzleScript's directly retrieved documentation index links a tool for extracting source code from exported standalone games. Standalone export therefore belongs in the existing comparison rather than being treated as absent. The linked extraction page failed to fetch, and no exported game was executed. The index alone does not establish offline behavior, reproducible builds or independence from every remote dependency. The page is undated and its exact cutoff version was not checked.

observed.claim: GDC’s 2026 survey summary reports AI use by 30% of game-studio respondents versus 58% at publishers and support/marketing firms, chiefly for brainstorming, emails, coding help and prototypes. It reports Unreal as the primary engine for 42% of developers and Unity for 30%. These are survey reports, not measured productivity; fieldwork and publication dates are unspecified.

On September 11, 2026, Roblox reported about 9,000 games published through September 1 using its mobile prompt-to-game Build alpha. Of those who created a game, 71% had never used Roblox Studio. Access was limited and expanding. Publishing is company-reported; lasting audiences, revenue and professional quality were not established.

Roblox reports over 160,000 Wish Master objects using predefined structures and scripted behavior, with trouble interpreting unexpected wishes. Stronger research analogues exist: GROMIT reports runtime-generated behavior code; World Crafting describes a restricted-language spell prototype. Only source-extracted text was inspected for these additions; commercial persistence remains unverified.

In an August 23, 2026 retrospective, Inselnova’s maker reports six months building a multiplayer browser game with AI writing most code, using existing game foundations and 30 years of software experience. He reports around 1,000 players. Automated design improvement failed; he personally tests beyond basic automated checks. This is one unaudited account.

DeepMind’s undated Genie page describes prompt-driven interactive environments, but limits continuous interaction to a few minutes and actions to a limited range. It calls interaction among independent agents unsolved. This is a vendor description, not evidence of a production game-making tool or deployed multiplayer; the page’s exact cutoff version is uncertain.

On July 9, 2025, SAG-AFTRA reported ratifying a video-game agreement requiring consent and disclosure for AI replicas of covered performers, with strike-related consent rights. This is a historical negotiated protection, not a universal restriction on synthetic voices. The announcement was inspected through an extracted search result; later enforcement was not verified.

The inspected, undated Steamworks rules require disclosure of AI-made content players receive and safeguards for content generated during play. Developers retain responsibility for non-infringement and managing recurring AI-service costs. Ordinary tool-efficiency gains are distinguished from shipped content. Compliance and profitability are not measured; a cutoff archive was not checked.

METR’s February 24, 2026 update says its coding experiment begun in August 2025 cannot reliably estimate current productivity effects. Participants withheld tasks or refused work without AI, pay changed, and simultaneous AI work complicated timing. Its older slowdown result is not a current capability baseline. Participants were open-source developers, not game-production teams.

METR’s February–April 2026 survey of 349 technical workers found perceived median speed gains of three times, but smaller perceived gains in work value. Its May 11 report warns that the convenience sample and low email response limit interpretation, and preliminary checks questioned large claims. These are perceptions, not measured game-production gains.

Roblox reported on September 11, 2026 that developers earned over $1.5 billion through its cash-payout program in the year ending June 30, up over 60%. It also reported more games reaching one million monthly users. These company totals show aggregate earnings and reach, not typical creator income, profit or an effect caused by AI.

A Kotaku report dated January 9, 2026 quotes Larian abandoning AI concept-art tools while using models trained on its own data to adjust captured actors’ motion for cinematic scenes. This distinguishes asset creation from production assistance at one studio. Only a truncated indexed excerpt was inspected; the original discussion and subsequent game delivery were not checked.

PuzzleScript executes explicit rules, documents manual loop repair and references standalone exports. BIPED reports playable prototypes plus formal analysis from one definition; SPIN research reports property checks and animated traces. Research was inspected via indexed excerpts. Routine commercial nonprogrammer delivery, mandatory conflict resolution and full reproducibility remain unverified.

Adventure Lab advertises paid, live-performer VR adventures for up to eight players. Its site also says public shows are unavailable and invites private inquiries. Human-hosted play already exists, but current bookings, sustainable revenue and live geometry editing were not verified.

Archipelago already connects different games through items that affect progress. Users can generate and host experiences, developers can add integrations, and a release system lets others continue when a player leaves. Broad host permissions, version guarantees and general world-state transfers were not established.

Second Life documentation describes scripts with permission-controlled effects on money, movement and objects. Only indexed source text was inspected for this finding. It does not establish the share of player-made activities or guarantees for preserving dependent, abandoned creations.

Dwarf Fortress documentation describes simulated histories that change playable starting conditions and continue during play. History length and stopping choices influence the resulting world. Large-batch production searches, causal debugging and the extent of unanticipated solutions were not established.

unknowns: Evidence is concentrated on AI assistance and Roblox; it does not cover the full range of ways people make video games.
Current workflows, costs and working conditions across large studios, small teams, hobbyists, countries and platforms are not established.
The evidence does not establish how generation tools connect to sustained design, testing, release, maintenance and earning a living across the industry.
Several sources are undated or have unknown observation periods; their precise timing and version at the cutoff remain uncertain.
Measured effects on total development time, budgets, game quality and staffing are unknown. Coding surveys and individual accounts do not resolve them.
Whether people entering through prompt-to-game tools keep making games, attract returning players or earn money is not established.
Roblox’s full Build–Studio connection remained unfinished in September 2026; its Scene Generator was promised for later in 2026, not established as delivered.
The cost and reliability of generating content during play over long sessions, including multiplayer, are not established.
How widely studios can document permission to use training material, generated assets and performers’ replicas—and how rules are enforced—is not established.
The evidence does not establish whether AI contributed to reported layoffs, changed hiring requirements or redistributed income among game makers.
The supplied sources do not establish whether existing engines, stores and studio arrangements will persist, change or be replaced by 2030.
GROMIT and World Crafting strengthen the runtime-invention comparison, but paid deployment, generated locations and enforced multi-session consequences remain unverified.
Whether current runtime-generation projects primarily author constraints, examples and world memory is unknown; retrieved prototype descriptions do not measure production work.
BIPED and SPIN research strengthen the checking comparison; present nonprogrammer conflict-resolution workflows and affordable complete state coverage remain unverified.
PuzzleScript documents standalone exports, but inspected evidence does not establish reproducible offline delivery in a complete checked-rule commercial workflow.

commitments.statement: By December 2030, multiple paid games create executable actions and locations during play that were not enumerated before release.
In those games, generated actions alter persistent world state and constrain later events across multiple sessions.
Their makers primarily author constraints, examples and world memory rather than prebuilding every supported gameplay branch.
Their production teams maintain live consistency and safety checks because testing a fixed pre-release game cannot cover the delivered experience.

consequences.mechanism: An invented action matters beyond its first appearance only if its effects survive and limit what can happen later. Without executable invention, this becomes ordinary persistence of prewritten mechanics.

When new mechanics can enter a continuing world after release, a finished pre-release test suite cannot inspect every delivered combination. Teams must check new behavior against existing state during operation. Cost and inconsistent state could make this impractical.

comparisons.present_match: Wish Master generates functional objects within predefined structures and scripts; Genie generates short interactive environments.
comparisons.remaining_difference: New executable actions beyond those structures remain different from these matches; stronger current runtime systems remain undercovered.

comparisons.present_match: No retrieved comparison established multi-session state constrained by newly generated mechanics.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Persistence of invented rules, rather than remembered narrative alone, remains unverified.

comparisons.present_match: Supplied tools expose prompts and predefined object behavior, but not a verified primarily constraint-authored production workflow.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The actual division between writing boundaries and implementing branches is unknown.

present_analogue.statement: Wish Master already lets players request functional generated objects, but inspected evidence describes predefined structures with scripted behavior. Genie generates interactive environments but reports short interaction windows and limited actions. These are partial analogues, not demonstrated long-running games that invent executable mechanics and preserve their consequences. Searches for runtime code generation did not establish a stronger match; that gap remains unknown.

falsifiers: Generated content remains cosmetic while all consequential actions come from a fixed menu.
The cost or inconsistency of live generation prevents sustained paid use.
endpoints.original_narrative: Imagine playing a detective game and deciding to become the suspect's landlord. The game invents a workable rental system while preserving the clues and characters you already know. Its maker wrote the world's constraints, not that branch. Making such a game means shaping what can change, what must remain true and when improvisation must stop. Small teams can offer enormous freedom, but there is no complete walkthrough or fixed object for reviewers to inspect. Bad memory or inconsistent rules would turn apparent freedom into nonsense.
endpoints.original_statement: In this imagined 2030, a commercial category of games generates places, encounters and available actions during play. Makers publish a world's rules and creative boundaries rather than a finished sequence of content. A player can attempt an unforeseen action without waiting for a developer to add it.
signals: Trials in which unforeseen player actions become working mechanics rather than dialogue alone.
Long play sessions that preserve generated facts and consequences without manual repair.
endpoints.title: Some games are performed by software rather than built in advance

commitments.statement: By December 2030, nonprogrammers routinely publish complete commercial puzzle or strategy games from explicit rules and examples without editing implementation code.
In this category, production systems check stated properties such as puzzle reachability, resource conservation and legal turn order across all modeled states.
When requirements conflict, these systems present concrete counterexamples and require creators to resolve the conflicting design choices.
The resulting games run as fixed, reproducible releases without requiring their original generation service.

consequences.mechanism: A check that finds incompatible requirements must return a specific failing situation if the creator is to choose which rule to change. Without that feedback, the system can silently choose an interpretation instead of preserving design control.

In this proposed workflow, checks and understandable counterexamples let creators repair design choices rather than implementation code. Removing them leaves the main proposed route to reliable nonprogrammer completion missing. They still cannot establish that a game is enjoyable.

comparisons.present_match: PuzzleScript executes authored rules; Roblox Build reports publishing games by people new to Studio.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Neither finding establishes routine complete commercial production from rules and examples without implementation repair.

comparisons.present_match: Archipelago constrains item placement for reachability; PuzzleScript documents a manually corrected infinite loop.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Checking requested properties across every modeled state is stronger than constrained generation or manual rule debugging.

comparisons.present_match: No retrieved source established game builders that require authors to resolve concrete conflicting requirements.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Current counterexample-guided game-authoring coverage is incomplete; failed searches do not establish novelty.

comparisons.present_match: The inspected rule-engine documentation did not establish release independence from its authoring or generation service.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Service-independent delivery in the proposed end-to-end arrangement remains unverified.

game rules formal verification counterexamples puzzle generation commercial standalone

present_analogue.statement: PuzzleScript already makes playable puzzles from explicit behavior rules. Roblox Build reports prompt-made published games, while Archipelago uses generation rules to keep progress items accessible. These challenge the broad idea of making games by specifying rules. None of the inspected findings establishes the complete proposed combination: nonprogrammer commercial delivery, all-modeled-state checks, concrete design-conflict counterexamples and service-independent releases.

falsifiers: Generated games still require programmers to repair ordinary interactions.
Checks cover code errors but cannot establish the gameplay properties creators request.
endpoints.original_narrative: Imagine a teacher making a cooperative mystery over a weekend. She specifies that every puzzle must remain solvable after any permitted item trade and that two players must contribute to the ending. A production system generates the game, finds a contradiction and asks her which rule to change. The finished download runs without a generation service. Designers spend more time inventing and resolving rules; repeatable releases are easy to archive and modify. This works only where the game's important behavior can be expressed precisely.
endpoints.original_statement: In this imagined 2030, people make bounded games by describing rules, examples and forbidden outcomes. Software turns these into complete, fixed releases and checks important properties before publication. Creation moves toward deciding precisely what a game should allow, rather than manually implementing each interaction.
signals: End-to-end game builders that expose contradictions rather than silently choosing an interpretation.
Creators shipping reliable games from restricted rule languages.
endpoints.title: Creators specify rules and receive complete, checkable games

commitments.statement: By December 2030, multiple persistent games let ordinary players create executable mechanics inside the shared live world, not only cosmetic objects or separate maps.
In those games, player-built systems supply most newly introduced playable activities over at least one continuous year.
Player creations can depend on other players' live infrastructure and state, allowing changes in one creation to affect activities elsewhere.
These worlds provide permissions, rollback and transfer of abandoned creations sufficient to keep shared dependencies operating without their original builders.

consequences.mechanism: Working creations can become inputs to someone else's activity because they change shared state. If player objects are only decorative or isolated, another player's railway timetable cannot govern a rescue game.

Once other activities rely on a creation, sabotage or abandonment can break more than its owner's work. Recovery, permissions and transfer become operating needs rather than optional editing conveniences. Their sufficiency remains unproven.

comparisons.present_match: Second Life scripts perform consequential actions; Wish Master lets players generate functional objects with scripted behavior.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The full ordinary-player creation workflow across multiple persistent games was not verified. Functional in-world making is not itself new.

comparisons.present_match: No retrieved source measures the share of newly introduced activities supplied by players for a continuous year.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The majority claim needs a defined activity measure and longitudinal evidence.

comparisons.present_match: Script permissions show consequential actions but do not establish dependencies between independently maintained live creations.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The strongest shared-infrastructure examples were not adequately retrieved.

comparisons.present_match: Second Life documents permissions; the combined rollback, abandonment transfer and dependency-preservation claim was not established.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Permission control alone does not show that a dependent system survives its builder's departure.

Second Life scripting shared objects permissions transfer ownership

present_analogue.statement: Second Life's script documentation provides a stronger challenge than cosmetic user content: scripts can affect movement, money and objects under permission controls. Roblox's Wish Master also demonstrates constrained functional creation during play. These establish pieces of consequential in-world making. The inspected material does not establish player-built activity majorities, durable dependencies between creators, or recovery and transfer of abandoned infrastructure.

falsifiers: Player content remains isolated in separate sessions with no consequential shared state.
Abuse and broken dependencies force operators to restrict creation to decorative assets.
endpoints.original_narrative: Imagine logging in to discover that other players built a railway, invented freight insurance and started a dispute over a tunnel. You make a rescue game using the railway's actual timetable. It earns an audience because it belongs to the world people already inhabit. The studio maintains safe construction rules, recovery tools and limits on resource use. Player builders must support their creations because others rely on them. Without ways to contain sabotage and preserve abandoned work, the accumulating world becomes unusable.
endpoints.original_statement: In this imagined 2030, some large persistent games stop receiving most playable content through studio expansions. Players create working institutions, machines, quests and places inside the ongoing world. Their creations become shared dependencies, making game development resemble maintaining a inhabited town rather than releasing a sequence of products.
signals: Players maintaining services that other creators use as functioning parts of their games.
World operators measuring content growth through player construction rather than expansion releases.
endpoints.title: Players make the next version of the world while living in it

commitments.statement: By December 2030, an ecosystem spanning independently maintained games exposes supported actions and state changes that outside creators can combine into playable campaigns.
Those campaigns transfer consequential resources, capabilities or world changes across games, rather than only identity, achievements or cosmetic items.
Creators who do not operate the host games can publish and maintain complete cross-game experiences through documented permissions and interfaces.
The ecosystem provides version support, validation of transferred outcomes and defined behavior when a host game becomes unavailable.

consequences.mechanism: A supported connection can turn an outcome in one game into a usable input in another. Without that connection, creators can link stories or ask players to report results, but cannot deliver dependable shared consequences.

An outside author's campaign can break when a host changes an action, rejects a result or goes offline. Version handling and fallback rules preserve the playable chain. Archipelago already solves part of this problem, so a future date or new distribution channel is not a sufficient difference.

comparisons.present_match: Archipelago combines supported games into a unified multiplayer experience through game integrations.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The core cross-game system exists; broad host-endorsed action interfaces were not established.

comparisons.present_match: Items found in one game are sent to another game and can be necessary for the receiving player to progress.
comparisons.remaining_difference: No difference for consequential item and capability transfer; general changes to host worlds were not established.

comparisons.present_match: Users generate and host experiences; outside developers can consult documentation and example integrations.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Documented permission from host operators and the full proposed campaign-authoring freedom remain unverified.

comparisons.present_match: Archipelago has reachability rules and a release system that sends remaining items when someone leaves.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Broad version support, validation of outcomes and behavior for host-game outages go beyond the inspected guarantees.

Archipelago multiworld randomizer items games API

present_analogue.statement: Archipelago already combines separately developed games into a shared experience: an item found in one game can unlock progress in another. Users generate and host sessions, developers add integrations, and a release mechanism prevents a departing player from trapping others. This is consequential cross-game play, not cosmetic portability. The remaining distinction would have to concern supported host permissions, broader action interfaces and dependable compatibility—not the basic idea of connecting games.

falsifiers: Connections remain bespoke promotions controlled by a single publisher.
Balance, security or commercial disputes restrict transfers to cosmetics and badges.
endpoints.original_narrative: Imagine making a rescue campaign without building vehicles, cities or battles. You connect three existing games: supplies won in a race repair a bridge in a construction game, opening an evacuation route in a strategy game. Each host exposes a limited set of dependable actions and outcomes. Your job is to design their relationship and handle players who own only part of the chain. Hosts gain new uses but surrender some control over context. Unstable rules, cheating or incompatible updates could unravel the whole experience.
endpoints.original_statement: In this imagined 2030, a connected game ecosystem lets independent makers compose new experiences from existing games' working systems. A creator can make a campaign that crosses a racing world, a building world and a strategy world while preserving meaningful consequences. Compatibility becomes a creative medium, not just a way to move costumes.
signals: Game operators supporting external use of consequential mechanics rather than asset exports alone.
Players buying campaigns whose main creative contribution is the relationship between existing games.
endpoints.title: Creators build games that span other people's games

commitments.statement: By December 2030, multiple game businesses earn recurring revenue from scheduled multiplayer sessions whose story decisions are controlled live by paid human performers.
Performers can alter spaces, objectives and character relationships during sessions without requiring a programmer or restarting play.
These businesses produce reusable settings and rehearse improvisational situations rather than authoring every offered story branch.
Human performance capacity determines ticket availability and operating costs in this category, rather than being occasional promotional support.

consequences.mechanism: If performers can change the playable situation rather than only recite dialogue, makers must prepare reusable situations and practice responding to choices. Without that control, the performance can sit on top of a substantially fixed game.

Every offered session needs human attention. Removing the live performer removes the labor bottleneck that ties ticket supply and operating costs to the number of sessions. Customers may not pay enough to cover that work.

comparisons.present_match: Adventure Lab advertises paid multiplayer VR adventures directed by a responsive live performer.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The core paid format exists. Multiple businesses' recurring revenue is unverified; scale alone would not make a new mechanism.

comparisons.present_match: Adventure Lab documents reactive performers, not in-session rebuilding of spaces and objectives.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Whether performers already make all these changes without programming or restarting remains unknown.

comparisons.present_match: The advertised repeatable setting and improvisation do not reveal rehearsal practices or the extent of prewritten branches.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The claimed production method needs direct operational evidence.

comparisons.present_match: Adventure Lab's format requires a live performer for a limited-size session; public shows are presently unavailable.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Human presence is already central. Actual staffing, ticket constraints and operating costs across businesses remain unverified.

Adventure Lab Dr Crumb live host VR tickets

present_analogue.statement: Adventure Lab already offers an adventure format combining multiplayer VR, paying guests and a live improvisational performer who responds to the group. The basic human-performed game experience is therefore not new. Its site currently says public shows are unavailable, with private bookings by inquiry. The proposed distinction would have to rest on meaningful live control of spaces and objectives and a durable production arrangement, not merely tickets, actors or a future date.

falsifiers: Customers will not pay enough to sustain the human staff.
Live interventions remain limited to dialogue or prewritten event triggers.
endpoints.original_narrative: Imagine booking a two-hour heist with five friends. Behind the characters, a small troupe watches your argument and turns a minor guard into a potential ally. An operator reshapes the building without breaking its doors or objectives. The same setting supports very different evenings, so makers rehearse situations rather than finish branching scripts. Actors and hosts become part of the production team. Attendance limits, labor costs and the difficulty of training good improvisers keep this from becoming an unlimited-content service.
endpoints.original_statement: In this imagined 2030, live game troupes become an established way to make multiplayer adventures. Human performers control motives, reversals and social situations while software handles scenery, movement and routine characters. Players buy a scheduled experience that can respond meaningfully to their group's choices.
signals: Repeat purchases for human-directed sessions rather than merely human-voiced characters.
Live editing tools that preserve playable state while operators change the situation.
endpoints.title: Game makers run live performances instead of selling finished adventures

criteria.changed_arrangement: Cited present analogue is supported in its actual scope, and the defining commitments specify materially changed capabilities, experiences or causal operation with dependent consequences. Institutional change is not required. Adoption counts when it enables such a change, not merely greater availability or prevalence.
criteria.present_or_adoption_only: The defining mechanism and its claimed capabilities or experiences already exist in the compared setting, or only price, distribution, prevalence, packaging or convenience changes without a consequential difference in what becomes possible or how it works.
criteria.unresolved: A consequential present-relative change is not established.
criteria.unsupported_analogue: The cited material does not substantiate the claimed present analogue or necessary scope contrast; absence of evidence is not evidence of novelty.

result.instructions:
A world changes what becomes possible or impossible to do or experience, or how the relevant system actually works, with interacting consequences that answer the user's question. Social or economic arrangements matter when they change those capabilities, experiences or causal operation; they are not required. A new tool, process or medium can be a defining mechanism when its capabilities change the whole answer. Renaming a device, adding decorative scenes or changing ownership does not by itself establish a consequential change. Distinct worlds may share tools or institutions while producing materially different capabilities, experiences and causal paths.

Challenge the chosen analogue against ALL supplied source findings: an uncited stronger present match overrides a weak selected comparison. Check each defining commitment against the strongest relevant existing capabilities, experiences and causal mechanisms, including the present frontier rather than only average adoption. A supported example does not establish that it is closest. A currently published report may project future outcomes: its publication and forecast are evidence only of what the source reports, not that the projected arrangement exists. Preserve claim_type, provenance, source_correction, observation dates and textual qualifications; do not classify a projected outcome as a present counterexample. Reported queries are researcher self-report, not independently verified search or proof of absence. If necessary comparison coverage remains unknown, choose unresolved. Preserve scope/date caveats. Do not award novelty for low probability, future dates, narrative length, or unsupported claims about today's absence. A familiar mechanism under changed conditions may qualify if its newly enabled capabilities or consequences are explicit and supported by the present comparison.

observed.claim: GDC’s 2026 survey summary reports AI use by 30% of game-studio respondents versus 58% at publishers and support/marketing firms, chiefly for brainstorming, emails, coding help and prototypes. It reports Unreal as the primary engine for 42% of developers and Unity for 30%. These are survey reports, not measured productivity; fieldwork and publication dates are unspecified.

On September 11, 2026, Roblox reported about 9,000 games published through September 1 using its mobile prompt-to-game Build alpha. Of those who created a game, 71% had never used Roblox Studio. Access was limited and expanding. Publishing is company-reported; lasting audiences, revenue and professional quality were not established.

Roblox’s February 4, 2026 account reports players generating over 160,000 objects in Wish Master early access. Generation used predefined object structures, with scripts supplying behavior. The developer reported trouble interpreting unexpected wishes. This vendor-hosted account shows constrained in-game making, not reliable creation of arbitrary objects or games.

In an August 23, 2026 retrospective, Inselnova’s maker reports six months building a multiplayer browser game with AI writing most code, using existing game foundations and 30 years of software experience. He reports around 1,000 players. Automated design improvement failed; he personally tests beyond basic automated checks. This is one unaudited account.

DeepMind’s undated Genie page describes prompt-driven interactive environments, but limits continuous interaction to a few minutes and actions to a limited range. It calls interaction among independent agents unsolved. This is a vendor description, not evidence of a production game-making tool or deployed multiplayer; the page’s exact cutoff version is uncertain.

On July 9, 2025, SAG-AFTRA reported ratifying a video-game agreement requiring consent and disclosure for AI replicas of covered performers, with strike-related consent rights. This is a historical negotiated protection, not a universal restriction on synthetic voices. The announcement was inspected through an extracted search result; later enforcement was not verified.

The inspected, undated Steamworks rules require disclosure of AI-made content players receive and safeguards for content generated during play. Developers retain responsibility for non-infringement and managing recurring AI-service costs. Ordinary tool-efficiency gains are distinguished from shipped content. Compliance and profitability are not measured; a cutoff archive was not checked.

METR’s February 24, 2026 update says its coding experiment begun in August 2025 cannot reliably estimate current productivity effects. Participants withheld tasks or refused work without AI, pay changed, and simultaneous AI work complicated timing. Its older slowdown result is not a current capability baseline. Participants were open-source developers, not game-production teams.

METR’s February–April 2026 survey of 349 technical workers found perceived median speed gains of three times, but smaller perceived gains in work value. Its May 11 report warns that the convenience sample and low email response limit interpretation, and preliminary checks questioned large claims. These are perceptions, not measured game-production gains.

Roblox reported on September 11, 2026 that developers earned over $1.5 billion through its cash-payout program in the year ending June 30, up over 60%. It also reported more games reaching one million monthly users. These company totals show aggregate earnings and reach, not typical creator income, profit or an effect caused by AI.

A Kotaku report dated January 9, 2026 quotes Larian abandoning AI concept-art tools while using models trained on its own data to adjust captured actors’ motion for cinematic scenes. This distinguishes asset creation from production assistance at one studio. Only a truncated indexed excerpt was inspected; the original discussion and subsequent game delivery were not checked.

PuzzleScript already turns explicit pattern-replacement rules into playable puzzle behavior. Its documentation also illustrates an infinite loop requiring manual correction. This establishes rule-based authoring, not automatic all-state gameplay verification or routine commercial creation without implementation work.

Adventure Lab advertises paid, live-performer VR adventures for up to eight players. Its site also says public shows are unavailable and invites private inquiries. Human-hosted play already exists, but current bookings, sustainable revenue and live geometry editing were not verified.

Archipelago already connects different games through items that affect progress. Users can generate and host experiences, developers can add integrations, and a release system lets others continue when a player leaves. Broad host permissions, version guarantees and general world-state transfers were not established.

Second Life documentation describes scripts with permission-controlled effects on money, movement and objects. Only indexed source text was inspected for this finding. It does not establish the share of player-made activities or guarantees for preserving dependent, abandoned creations.

Dwarf Fortress documentation describes simulated histories that change playable starting conditions and continue during play. History length and stopping choices influence the resulting world. Large-batch production searches, causal debugging and the extent of unanticipated solutions were not established.

unknowns: Evidence is concentrated on AI assistance and Roblox; it does not cover the full range of ways people make video games.
Current workflows, costs and working conditions across large studios, small teams, hobbyists, countries and platforms are not established.
The evidence does not establish how generation tools connect to sustained design, testing, release, maintenance and earning a living across the industry.
Several sources are undated or have unknown observation periods; their precise timing and version at the cutoff remain uncertain.
Measured effects on total development time, budgets, game quality and staffing are unknown. Coding surveys and individual accounts do not resolve them.
Whether people entering through prompt-to-game tools keep making games, attract returning players or earn money is not established.
Roblox’s full Build–Studio connection remained unfinished in September 2026; its Scene Generator was promised for later in 2026, not established as delivered.
The cost and reliability of generating content during play over long sessions, including multiplayer, are not established.
How widely studios can document permission to use training material, generated assets and performers’ replicas—and how rules are enforced—is not established.
The evidence does not establish whether AI contributed to reported layoffs, changed hiring requirements or redistributed income among game makers.
The supplied sources do not establish whether existing engines, stores and studio arrangements will persist, change or be replaced by 2030.

consequences.mechanism: A supported connection can turn an outcome in one game into a usable input in another. Without that connection, creators can link stories or ask players to report results, but cannot deliver dependable shared consequences.

An outside author's campaign can break when a host changes an action, rejects a result or goes offline. Version handling and fallback rules preserve the playable chain. Archipelago already solves part of this problem, so a future date or new distribution channel is not a sufficient difference.

defining_commitments.statement: By December 2030, an ecosystem spanning independently maintained games exposes supported actions and state changes that outside creators can combine into playable campaigns.
Those campaigns transfer consequential resources, capabilities or world changes across games, rather than only identity, achievements or cosmetic items.
Creators who do not operate the host games can publish and maintain complete cross-game experiences through documented permissions and interfaces.
The ecosystem provides version support, validation of transferred outcomes and defined behavior when a host game becomes unavailable.

comparisons.present_match: Archipelago combines supported games into a unified multiplayer experience through game integrations.
comparisons.remaining_difference: The core cross-game system exists; broad host-endorsed action interfaces were not established.

comparisons.present_match: Items found in one game are sent to another game and can be necessary for the receiving player to progress.
comparisons.remaining_difference: No difference for consequential item and capability transfer; general changes to host worlds were not established.

comparisons.present_match: Users generate and host experiences; outside developers can consult documentation and example integrations.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Documented permission from host operators and the full proposed campaign-authoring freedom remain unverified.

comparisons.present_match: Archipelago has reachability rules and a release system that sends remaining items when someone leaves.
comparisons.remaining_difference: Broad version support, validation of outcomes and behavior for host-game outages go beyond the inspected guarantees.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://gdconf.com/article/gdc-2026-state-of-the-game-industry-reveals-impact-of-layoffs-generative-ai-and-more/ | 2026 report summary; article date unstated. “30% of respondents at game studios reported using AI tools”"]
source_evidence.statement: GDC’s 2026 survey summary reports generative-AI use by 36% of over 2,300 industry respondents, but 30% at game studios versus 58% at publishers, support and marketing/PR firms. Reported uses emphasize brainstorming, emails, code assistance and prototyping, not autonomous delivery of games. 52% judged its industry impact negative. This is self-reported use and sentiment in a changing sample, not a productivity test or frontier-capability ceiling. Exact fieldwork and article publication dates are not supplied on the inspected page.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://about.roblox.com/newsroom/2026/09/rdc-2026-the-world-needs-more-play | 2026-09-11 | “71% had never used Roblox Studio before”"]
source_evidence.statement: On September 11, 2026 Roblox reported that its mobile prompt-to-game Build alpha had published approximately 9,000 games through September 1; 71% of the thousands who created a game had never used Roblox Studio. Alpha access was expanding from New Zealand to Serbia, Singapore and conference attendees. This is company-reported actual publishing and entry by new Studio users, not proof of retained audiences, revenue or professional-grade games. Full Build–Studio integration remained work in progress and Scene Generator was still promised for later in 2026, updating July’s broader description of a shared workflow.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://about.roblox.com/newsroom/2026/02/accelerating-creation-powered-roblox-cube-foundation-model | 2026-02-04 | “Players would request things that didn’t exist”"]
source_evidence.statement: Roblox’s February 4, 2026 Cube beta account describes players generating functional objects inside Wish Master: over 160,000 objects during early access. The beta launched with a five-part car schema and a single-mesh object schema; scripts attach behavior and adapt to generated dimensions. Developer Laksh reported difficulties interpreting unexpected wishes and a 64% higher average play time among users engaging with 4D generation. This vendor-hosted developer account establishes constrained in-game making, not arbitrary reliable generation; the play-time comparison does not isolate a causal effect.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://inselnova.com/chronicle/2026-08-23-retrospective-building-with-ai/ | 2026-08-23 | “they only check the rules I gave them, not whether those rules are any good”"]
source_evidence.statement: In an August 23, 2026 first-person retrospective, Inselnova maker Darren reports building a live multiplayer browser game over six months with AI coding, initially on a phone and provider cloud, and attracting around 1,000 players. He has 30 years of software experience and built on an existing game’s foundations. He reports that AI writes most code, but his attempt to automate design improvement with Playwright failed; he now uses it for registration/tutorial checks and tests the rest himself. This is one experienced developer’s account, not an audited productivity or quality comparison; audience counts and bug-free claims were not independently tested.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://deepmind.google/models/genie/ | publication None | “a few minutes of continuous interaction, rather than extended hours”"]
source_evidence.statement: Google DeepMind’s inspected Genie model page describes interactive generated environments and prompt-driven changes to weather, objects and characters. It also explicitly limits continuous interaction to a few minutes, agent actions to a limited range, and describes interaction among multiple independent agents as an unsolved research challenge. This is a vendor capability/limitation description, not evidence of an editable production engine, hours-long games or deployed multiplayer. The page is undated and its exact version at the research cutoff cannot be independently established.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://www.sagaftra.org/sag-aftra-members-approve-2025-video-game-agreement | publication 2025-07-09 | “consent and disclosure requirements for A.I. digital replica use”"]
source_evidence.statement: Historical institutional baseline: on July 9, 2025 SAG-AFTRA reported ratification of its Interactive Media Agreement, ending the video game strike, with consent and disclosure requirements for AI digital replicas and a right to suspend consent for new material during strikes. These are negotiated protections for covered performers and employers, not a universal ban on synthetic game voices. Direct fetch failed; the substantive union announcement was inspected through a source-extracted search result. No later amendment or enforcement outcomes were verified.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/gettingstarted/contentsurvey | publication None | “Efficiency gains through the use of these tools is not the focus of this section.”"]
source_evidence.statement: The inspected Steamworks Content Survey distinguishes AI-made content shipped to players from ordinary tool-efficiency gains. It requires disclosure of pre-generated player-facing content and additional guardrail information for live generation; publishers still promise non-infringement. Its FAQ already addresses recurring AI-service costs, leaving developers to manage access and payment, and rejects live-generated adult-only sexual content. This establishes platform rules, not compliance rates or profitability. Documentation is undated; an archived October 3 version was not independently checked.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/ | publication 2026-02-24 | “our data is only very weak evidence for the size of this increase”"]
source_evidence.statement: METR’s February 24, 2026 update says its new coding-productivity experiment, begun August 2025, is unreliable as a current effect estimate: more developers refused no-AI work, 30–50% reported withholding some tasks, pay fell from $150 to $50/hour, and concurrent agents made time accounting difficult. Its historical February–June 2025 slowdown result therefore is not a current frontier baseline. METR suspects improvement but explicitly cannot reliably size it. These are open-source software developers, not a game-production experiment.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-11-ai-usage-survey/ | publication 2026-05-11 | “survey results are not necessarily grounded in reality”"]
source_evidence.statement: METR’s May 11, 2026 report of a February–April survey of 349 technical workers finds self-reported median work-value gains of 1.4–2 times versus speed gains of 3 times. It warns that perceptions need not match reality: respondents were a convenience sample, email response around 2%, and preliminary output checks questioned especially large claims. This is newer evidence of perceived usefulness and changed task choice, not measured game-production speed, displaced employment or a representative industry estimate.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://about.roblox.com/newsroom/2026/09/rdc-2026-the-world-needs-more-play | publication 2026-09-11 | “earned over $1.5 billion through our Developer Exchange program”"]
source_evidence.statement: Roblox’s September 11, 2026 conference report says developers earned over $1.5 billion through Developer Exchange in the 12 months ending June 30, up over 60% year over year. It also reports 80% more developer games achieving at least one million monthly active users in Q2 2026 than a year earlier. These are platform-reported aggregate earnings and reach, not median take-home income, profit or evidence that AI caused the growth. Newly announced higher payouts for certain verified US adult spending and new subscription/bundle tools are policy changes, not demonstrated income effects.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://gdconf.com/article/gdc-2026-state-of-the-game-industry-reveals-impact-of-layoffs-generative-ai-and-more/ | publication None | “Unreal Engine (42%) is the primary engine”"]
source_evidence.statement: GDC’s 2026 survey summary reports Unreal as the primary engine for 42% of developers and Unity for 30%; Unity is more common among older indies and Godot is used by 11% of newer indies. It also reports 28% laid off in the preceding two years and half saying their current or latest employer laid people off within the past year. This is a cross-sectional survey with broader inclusion of non-development roles, not proof of engine migration or AI-caused layoffs. Exact fieldwork and publication dates are absent from the inspected summary.

source_evidence.source_refs: ["https://kotaku.com/divinity-gen-ai-larian-bg3-reddit-ama-2000658429 | 2026-01-09 | indexed excerpt: “These models are trained exclusively with Larian data.”"]
source_evidence.statement: A January 9, 2026 Kotaku report quotes Larian’s Reddit AMA: the studio was abandoning generative-AI concept-art tools while continuing experiments elsewhere. Its machine-learning director described an existing cinematics pipeline using models trained on Larian data to clean, retarget and add motion around captured actors’ performances. This is a reported studio account, not an audit or proof of universal rejection/acceptance of AI. Direct fetch failed; the inspected indexed excerpt is truncated and the original AMA was not inspected. It supports a distinction between creative-asset provenance and production assistance, not subsequent delivery of Divinity.

source_evidence.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
source_evidence.quote: The engine looks for the pattern on the left, and replaces it with the one on the right.
source_evidence.statement: PuzzleScript's directly retrieved Rules 101 documentation describes a working engine in which creators express tile-based puzzle behavior through pattern-replacement rules. Examples change pushing, movement, disappearance and teleportation. It also shows a rule that causes an infinite loop and explains a manual correction. This establishes executable rule-based authoring, not automatic verification across all states, creator-facing counterexamples, or routine commercial publishing by nonprogrammers. The page is undated; its cutoff version was not independently checked.

source_evidence.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
source_evidence.quote: No public shows are available at this time.
source_evidence.statement: Adventure Lab's directly retrieved site offers VR adventures with live improvisational performers, paying guests, up to eight players and a 60-minute format. It says performers guide the adventure and react to the team. However, the same page says no public shows are currently available and directs private-show inquiries to email. It establishes an actual paid human-hosted game arrangement, not verified current bookings, recurring profitability, multiple sustainable businesses, or live alteration of geometry and objectives. The page is undated and its current booking operation was not independently checked.

source_evidence.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
source_evidence.quote: If a player must leave early, they can use Archipelago's release system.
source_evidence.statement: Archipelago's directly retrieved FAQ explains cross-game multiplayer in which finding an item in one game sends it to another player's different game, affecting progress. Users can generate and host experiences; developer documentation and example game implementations are linked. A release system sends a departing player's outstanding items so others can continue. Generation rules aim to keep necessary items accessible. This is a strong existing analogue for consequential cross-game composition, including a departure fallback. It does not establish host-operator permission for every integration, general world-state editing, comprehensive version guarantees, or recovery from every host outage. The documentation is undated.

source_evidence.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
source_evidence.statement: An inspected source-extracted search result from Second Life's llRequestPermissions documentation describes executable scripts requesting permission for consequential actions, including taking money, controlling avatars, changing links, teleporting and returning objects. Permissions persist across script state changes but have specific limits, including one agent per script. This supports existing permission-controlled behavior inside a shared world, not evidence that ordinary players supply most new activities, that creations have durable shared dependencies, or that abandoned systems can be transferred and repaired. Direct retrieval of the related creation documentation failed. Page date and exact cutoff version remain unverified.

source_evidence.evidence_note: Retrieved report, not proof of a future event.
source_evidence.quote: These activities continue even after world generation, as you play the game.
source_evidence.statement: The directly retrieved Dwarf Fortress Wiki world-generation page describes simulated geography, civilizations and character histories that shape starting conditions and continue during play. Creators or players can select history length and interrupt generation when desired conditions occur; longer histories change the surviving settlements, creatures and other available features. This is an existing mechanism for obtaining playable situations from simulated history. The retrieved portion does not establish large-batch searches in multiple commercial production pipelines, comprehensive causal debugging, or specific unanticipated player solutions. The community page identifies a current game version but warns some content may need updating; its cutoff version was not checked.
